Electron-Phonon Coupling

QTrans evaluates electron-phonon coupling (EPC) by combining real-space Hamiltonian derivatives, atomic orbital expansion coefficients, and phonon eigenvectors. The formulation accounts for the motion and nonorthogonality of the atomic orbital basis [1]. Long-range electrostatic contributions can be added for polar and quadrupolar interactions.

Matrix Element and Phonon Convention

The EPC matrix element connects an initial Bloch state \(|\nu\mathbf{k}\rangle\) to a final state \(|\mu\mathbf{k+q}\rangle\) through phonon branch \(b\):

\[g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) = \langle\mu\mathbf{k+q}|\Delta_{\mathbf{q}b}\hat{\mathcal{H}} |\nu\mathbf{k}\rangle.\]

We use the electronic Bloch convention of Hamiltonian in an Atomic Orbital Basis. For a phonon with angular frequency \(\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}>0\), define

\[\ell_{\kappa,\mathbf{q}b} = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\mathbf{q}b}}}, \qquad \widetilde{e}_{\kappa\sigma}^{\mathbf{q}b} = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}_\kappa} e_{\kappa\sigma}^{\mathbf{q}b},\]

where \(M_\kappa\) and \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_\kappa\) are the mass and unit-cell position of atom \(\kappa\), and \(\sigma\) is a Cartesian direction. The vectors \(e^{\mathbf{q}b}\) are the normalized eigenvectors of the mass-weighted dynamical matrix returned by Phonopy, with \(\sum_{\kappa\sigma}|e_{\kappa\sigma}^{\mathbf{q}b}|^2=1\). The explicit atomic phase in \(\widetilde{e}\) matches the code’s phonon convention.

Let \(u_{p\kappa\sigma}\) denote the displacement of atom \(\kappa\) in cell \(p\). The phonon perturbation is

\[\Delta_{\mathbf{q}b}\hat{\mathcal{H}} = \sum_{p\kappa\sigma} \ell_{\kappa,\mathbf{q}b} \widetilde{e}_{\kappa\sigma}^{\mathbf{q}b} \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_p} \frac{\partial\hat{\mathcal{H}}}{\partial u_{p\kappa\sigma}}.\]

This definition gives \(g\) units of energy. With Bloch states normalized over \(N\) cells, the corresponding second-quantized interaction contains the conventional overall factor \(1/\sqrt{N}\):

\[\hat{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{ep}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{kq}\mu\nu b} g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) \hat{c}_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}^\dagger\hat{c}_{\nu\mathbf{k}} (\hat{b}_{\mathbf{q}b}+\hat{b}_{-\mathbf{q}b}^\dagger).\]

Here, \(\hat c\) and \(\hat b\) are electron and phonon annihilation operators, respectively, with consistent phases for the modes at \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(-\mathbf{q}\).

Real-Space Interpolation

Translational symmetry allows all displacement derivatives to be referred to atoms in the central unit cell. Define

\[G^{\kappa\sigma}_{mi\alpha,nj\beta} = \left\langle\phi_{mi\alpha}\left| \frac{\partial\hat{\mathcal{H}}}{\partial u_{0\kappa\sigma}} \right|\phi_{nj\beta}\right\rangle,\]

where \(m,n\) label lattice cells, \(i,j\) label atoms, and \(\alpha,\beta\) label orbitals. The EPC is then

\[\begin{split}g_{\mu\nu b}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) ={}& \sum_{mn}\sum_{i\alpha,j\beta}\sum_{\kappa\sigma} \ell_{\kappa,\mathbf{q}b} \widetilde{e}_{\kappa\sigma}^{\mathbf{q}b} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{k+q})\cdot\mathbf{R}_m} \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}_n} \\ &\times(C_{i\alpha}^{\mathbf{k+q},\mu})^* G^{\kappa\sigma}_{mi\alpha,nj\beta} C_{j\beta}^{\mathbf{k},\nu}.\end{split}\]

The conjugated coefficient and negative Bloch phase belong to the final state, while the unconjugated coefficient and positive phase belong to the initial state. Both cell indices are retained because displacing one atom breaks translational symmetry locally.

Unlike the band velocity, which uses analytic wave-vector derivatives, EPC requires derivatives with respect to atomic displacements. Once the real-space gradient tensor is prepared, the interpolation above can be evaluated at arbitrary electronic and phonon wave vectors.

Moving-Basis Corrections

The derivative of an atomic orbital Hamiltonian matrix element is not equal to the matrix element of the derivative operator, because the orbitals move with their parent atoms. For compact notation, use composite orbital indices \(I=(m,i,\alpha)\) and \(J=(n,j,\beta)\), and write \(\partial_{\kappa\sigma}=\partial/\partial u_{0\kappa\sigma}\). Then

\[\partial_{\kappa\sigma}H_{IJ} = \langle\partial_{\kappa\sigma}\phi_I| \hat{\mathcal{H}}|\phi_J\rangle +G^{\kappa\sigma}_{IJ} +\langle\phi_I|\hat{\mathcal{H}}| \partial_{\kappa\sigma}\phi_J\rangle.\]

Define the one-sided overlap derivative and auxiliary matrices by

\[\begin{split}D^{\kappa\sigma}_{IJ} &= \langle\phi_I|\partial_{\kappa\sigma}\phi_J\rangle, \\ A^{\kappa\sigma} &= D^{\kappa\sigma}-\partial_{\kappa\sigma}S = -(D^{\kappa\sigma})^\dagger, \\ B^{\kappa\sigma} &= (A^{\kappa\sigma})^\dagger=-D^{\kappa\sigma},\end{split}\]

where \(\partial_{\kappa\sigma}S=D^{\kappa\sigma}+(D^{\kappa\sigma})^\dagger\). Using the inverse overlap matrix within the finite atomic orbital space gives

\[G^{\kappa\sigma} = \partial_{\kappa\sigma}H + A^{\kappa\sigma}S^{-1}H + HS^{-1}(A^{\kappa\sigma})^\dagger.\]

The matrices in this expression act on the full set of supercell orbitals. The overlap matrix must be invertible. This is the moving-basis correction implemented when constructing the gradient tensor; using \(\partial_{\kappa\sigma}H\) alone omits the two basis-response terms.

For clarity, the matrix element of \(B\) has the ordered indices

\[B^{\kappa\sigma}_{IJ} = (A^{\kappa\sigma}_{JI})^*, \qquad \langle\partial_{\kappa\sigma}\phi_I|\phi_J\rangle = \partial_{\kappa\sigma}S_{IJ}+B^{\kappa\sigma}_{IJ}.\]

The overlap on the right has the same bra and ket ordering as the left-hand side. For real matrices, the adjoint reduces to a transpose; complex spinor matrices require the conjugate transpose.

Finite-Displacement Preparation

The preparation workflow obtains \(\partial H\) and \(\partial S\) from displaced supercells, using either forward differences,

\[\partial_{\kappa\sigma}H \simeq\frac{H(+\Delta u_{\kappa\sigma})-H(0)}{\Delta u},\]

or central differences,

\[\partial_{\kappa\sigma}H \simeq\frac{H(+\Delta u_{\kappa\sigma}) -H(-\Delta u_{\kappa\sigma})}{2\Delta u},\]

with analogous expressions for \(\partial S\). The input fd_method selects forward or central, and epc_sc_disp sets the displacement in angstrom. Forward differences are first-order accurate in \(\Delta u\); central differences are second-order accurate for smooth matrix elements.

The auxiliary matrix \(A\) is assembled from overlap derivatives and additional on-site orbital derivative overlaps. On-site terms require separate treatment because moving both orbitals together leaves their overlap unchanged even when a one-sided derivative is nonzero. The corrected \(G\) tensor is stored for subsequent EPC calculations. Its units are energy per length, internally Hartree per Bohr. Dense and sparse storage represent the same contraction; sparse thresholding introduces an additional numerical approximation.

Long-Range Electrostatic Correction

A finite real-space interpolation does not reproduce the nonanalytic long-wavelength field of a polar displacement. QTrans can add analytic long-range terms to the local EPC:

\[g_{\mu\nu b}=g^{\mathrm{local}}_{\mu\nu b} +g^{\mathrm{LR}}_{\mu\nu b}.\]

The contributions are added as complex amplitudes before taking \(|g|^2\), so their interference is retained. This decomposition assumes that the supplied local gradient and the analytic correction use a consistent separation of local and long-range contributions.

Three-Dimensional Correction

In atomic units, the implemented three-dimensional dipole and quadrupole correction can be expressed as

\[\begin{split}g^{\mathrm{LR}}_{\mu\nu b} ={}& \frac{4\pi}{V_{\mathrm{uc}}} \sum_{\kappa\sigma}\ell_{\kappa,\mathbf{q}b} \widetilde e_{\kappa\sigma}^{\mathbf{q}b} \sum_{\mathbf G}^{\mathbf Q\ne0} \frac{\exp[-d(\mathbf Q)/\eta_{\mathrm E}]}{d(\mathbf Q)} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\mathbf Q\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_\kappa} \mathcal{M}^{(t)}_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf Q) \\ &\times\left[ \mathrm{i}\sum_a Q_a Z^*_{\kappa,a\sigma} +\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ac}Q_a \mathcal Q_{\kappa,\sigma ac}Q_c\right],\end{split}\]

where \(\mathbf Q=\mathbf q+\mathbf G\) contains the physical \(2\pi\) factor, \(V_{\mathrm{uc}}\) is the unit-cell volume, \(Z^*\) is the Born effective charge tensor, and \(\mathcal Q\) is the dynamical quadrupole tensor in the code’s convention. The screened denominator is

\[d(\mathbf Q)=\mathbf Q\cdot\boldsymbol\epsilon_\infty\cdot\mathbf Q,\]

with the electronic dielectric tensor \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_\infty\). The positive parameter \(\eta_{\mathrm E}\) controls the Ewald damping; its units match \(d(\mathbf Q)\). The dipole and quadrupole terms are included only when their respective correction flags are enabled. With \(\mathcal Q=0\), the expression reduces to the dipole correction.

The electronic factor uses a Taylor approximation of the plane-wave operator in the atomic orbital basis. At order zero,

\[\mathcal M^{(0)}_{\mu\nu} = \mathbf C_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}^\dagger S^{\mathbf k}\mathbf C_{\nu\mathbf k}.\]

At order one, the code includes the position-matrix contribution:

\[\mathcal M^{(1)}_{\mu\nu} = \mathbf C_{\mu\mathbf{k+q}}^\dagger \left[\sum_n\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R_n} \left(S_{0,n}+\mathrm{i}\sum_aQ_a P^a_{0,n}\right)\right] \mathbf C_{\nu\mathbf k},\]

where \(P^a_{0,n}\) denotes the supplied atomic orbital position matrix. Orbital indices are suppressed in this expression. The parameter LRC_taylor_order selects order zero or one. The current three-dimensional order-one path supports only nonmagnetic calculations without spin-orbit coupling.

Two-Dimensional Correction

For system_2D, the code uses a separate screened two-dimensional interaction with \(q_z=0\). Its range-separation function is

\[f_L(Q)=1-\tanh(QL/2),\]

where \(L\) is set by range_separation_length_L. The in-plane and out-of-plane screening functions are

\[\begin{split}\epsilon_\parallel(\mathbf Q) &=1+\frac{2\pi f_L(Q)}{Q} \mathbf Q_\parallel\cdot\boldsymbol\alpha_\parallel \cdot\mathbf Q_\parallel, \\ \epsilon_\perp(Q) &=1-2\pi Qf_L(Q)\alpha_\perp,\end{split}\]

where \(\boldsymbol\alpha_\parallel\) and \(\alpha_\perp\) are the macroscopic sheet polarizabilities derived from the dielectric tensor and the specified supercell vacuum length. The two-dimensional Coulomb factor scales as \(2\pi f_L(Q)/(\mathcal A Q)\), with in-plane cell area \(\mathcal A\), instead of the three-dimensional \(4\pi/[V_{\mathrm{uc}}d(\mathbf Q)]\). The combined dipole/quadrupole implementation also uses an out-of-plane position-matrix contribution. It should not be replaced by the three-dimensional bulk expression for a slab separated by vacuum.

Numerical Settings and Output

The calculator reads the prepared gradient tensor from grad_mat_path. The real-space range is selected by cell_range_cut, and read_sparse_grad_mat chooses its storage format. Convergence should be checked with respect to the displacement, preparation supercell, retained real-space range, and sparse threshold.

The dipole and quadrupole corrections are controlled by apply_correction and quadrupole_correction. They require the corresponding Born charge, dielectric, and quadrupole data. The q_cut parameter limits where corrections are applied in the calling workflows.

Note

Phonon frequencies enter the factor \(\sqrt{\hbar/(2M_\kappa\omega_{\mathbf qb})}\). The code stores the phonon energy \(\hbar\omega\) in Hartree and masses in atomic units, giving the internal prefactor \(1/\sqrt{2M_\kappa E_{\mathbf qb}}\). Low-frequency branches are filtered using phonon_frequency_cutoff, entered in meV. Imaginary phonon modes require a structural-stability assessment; taking their absolute frequencies does not establish physical stability.

Note

The EPC path routine returns magnitudes \(|g|\) in Hartree. Its current small-wave-vector guard returns zero when the norm of the internal Cartesian wave vector is below \(10^{-6}\). This is a numerical convention, not the physical long-wavelength limit of a polar coupling. If path symmetrization is requested, the current implementation averages \(|g|^2\) over nearly degenerate phonon branches and returns its square root; it does not average over electronic degeneracies.
